en: OSMONDE, looking : These photos are excellent.
MICHEL : It's a good little camera.
OSMONDE : Look, father! (Claude looks over her shoulder.) What transparent light! And those pines against the sky!
MICHEL : You like pine trees?
OSMONDE : Do I like them! Father, remember, near Lake Chiberta. Their shape, their scent, and then, you know how the branches sway when the wind blows...
MICHEL, his voice altered : I too love all that very much.
CLAUDE, abruptly : Good heavens! My appointment!
EDMÉE : Don't go, then.
CLAUDE : Forstmeyer returned specially to see me.
EDMÉE : You don't know that at all.
CLAUDE : Already last time, I had to let him down.
EDMÉE : It wasn't your fault.

CLAUDE : No, it's impossible... (Awkwardly, to Michel.) If you had something particular to say to me, perhaps we could walk down together? (Michel does not answer.) It is true that it's only two steps away, we would hardly have the time... I am terribly sorry. Had I been warned earlier... (He seems at a loss.)
MICHEL, who has stood up : Perhaps we could arrange another appointment.
CLAUDE : But if you are leaving tomorrow?
MICHEL : It isn't decided yet.
CLAUDE : Then... You will arrange that with my wife... Goodbye, and forgive me for leaving you like this... (He exits.)
[SCENE IV]
MICHEL : I see that Monsieur Lemoyne is exceedingly busy.
OSMONDE : My father is too conscientious. (She holds out her hand to Michel.) Good evening, Monsieur.
MICHEL : Goodbye, Mademoiselle, very glad to have renewed our acquaintance. (Osmonde exits, Michel follows her with his eyes. A silence.)
EDMÉE, in a low voice : Why did you do that? (A vague gesture from Michel.) If it had been up to me, you would not have been received.
MICHEL : Ah!
EDMÉE : Now, I beg of you, leave!
MICHEL : Why?
EDMÉE : First because of the child... and then... I cannot bear to see you.

MICHEL : Is it because I haven't changed enough, or on the contrary...? Naturally, you know what has become of me. Besides, otherwise, I suppose he would not have tolerated... But as things stand, it was almost a professional obligation.
EDMÉE : Ah! Be quiet.

MICHEL : Decidedly distinguished, your husband, from every point of view. He cuts a fine figure... He looks the part... You say you cannot bear to see me. Well! As for me, it's very odd, being near you affects me not at all, absolutely not at all. Say what they will, all those literary men, there are parts of ourselves that are like dead skin, you could cut into them... and they wouldn't bleed. Besides, I recently had a curious experience. Opening the newspaper, I see: "Announcing the death of Madame Claude Lemoyne"... a namesake. Well, I cannot say... Really, it is so long ago; it didn't happen to us.
EDMÉE, staring blankly : Convenient.
MICHEL : I presume we die whole, but we live in pieces.
EDMÉE, bitterly : That may be true for men. I am the same.
MICHEL : You think so?
EDMÉE : Exactly the same.
MICHEL : And what does that mean?
EDMÉE : Oh! Conclude nothing from it. I suppose I have never loved anyone.
MICHEL : I arrived at that conclusion myself long ago; you have never loved anyone, and perhaps that's why...
EDMÉE : Why the announcement of my death didn't even make you start. (Gesture from Michel.)
MICHEL : Lately... well, ever since I have been completely certain of what awaits me... I have reviewed many faces; yours was among them.
EDMÉE : Among many others.
MICHEL : I didn't count... A cold face, tense, pitiless. Nor was it a courageous face, the eyes stared at the ground. They were dull. Oh, I suppose they shone sometimes, but I don't remember it.
EDMÉE : And since only memory is true...
MICHEL : Precisely. (A silence.)
EDMÉE : So I was supposed to have pitied you? No, that is truly extraordinary.

MICHEL : But since it didn't happen to us, don't you think it's pointless to bring up that story? If you only knew how stripped it is of all adornment for me. I see that... let's call it idyll... in a pallid light...
EDMÉE : It wasn't the light of Saint-Loup.
MICHEL : Perhaps.
EDMÉE : That after twenty years there should remain against me... such hostility! Why are you laughing?
MICHEL : Because that word is so ill-suited. You refuse to believe me when I tell you that now... But I did resent you, oh! Mortally so.
EDMÉE : So you loved me?
MICHEL : A remnant of me loved you, but since it is dead...
EDMÉE : Mere words.
MICHEL : If you only knew how little of what still lives in me amounts to... there isn't even enough to weep over the rest.
EDMÉE, with a trembling voice : I don't understand what you reproach me for. Good God! After twenty years, you are torturing me still...

MICHEL : I am torturing you? You were right a moment ago; you have remained the same... I remember that way you had of blaming me for the words you had just wrested from me. Besides, other women were just the same.
EDMÉE : Even back then, there were other women.
MICHEL : It pleased you to believe so, and I would feel scrupulous about disabusing you.
EDMÉE : I don't understand.
MICHEL : That scene of jealousy you made in that little station where we were shivering; one evening returning from Valence... (He shakes his head with a smile.)
EDMÉE : You mean to say I wasn't sincere?
MICHEL : All women are sincere; all women act in bad faith.
EDMÉE : One senses a wealth of experience.
MICHEL : I regret to tell you that since our breakup, I have not remained faithful to you.
EDMÉE : Besides, you made no secret of your intentions. Your letter...
MICHEL : My reply. I thought I understood that you were restoring my freedom.
EDMÉE : You certainly knew how to make the fullest use of it.
MICHEL : The fullest.
EDMÉE : How like you!
MICHEL : I made such broad use of that freedom you restored to me... well, that I am dying of it, that's all, it's very simple. And you can see there isn't the slightest tremor in my voice.
EDMÉE : My letter may have bruised you, but it did not contain a single word that should have festered.
MICHEL : The way you had gone and revealed our affair to your husband, and then that cowardly need for patching things up...
EDMÉE : Why cowardly? There was a risk.

MICHEL : There was none at all, and you knew it; what the devil! I remember what you used to say about your husband. No, you weighed everything, and you decided that moral comfort, security, peace of mind, what do I know...
EDMÉE : I weighed nothing. Suddenly that life of lies filled me with horror.
MICHEL : Just like that, all of a sudden?...
EDMÉE : Besides, if you had wanted to...
MICHEL : What?
EDMÉE : If you had offered to take me with you, I would have consented.
MICHEL : And yet, I did offer, and you refused.
EDMÉE : I felt you were hesitant; if you had insisted...

MICHEL : Don't you find it pathetic, even almost grotesque, this discussion over our youthful romance? Within three months I'll be in Père-Lachaise... and you! Good heavens, you could already be a grandmother. So really, I wonder...
EDMÉE : Earlier, when you said...
MICHEL : What?
EDMÉE : I don't want to repeat... that sentence about your freedom... It sounded as though you held me responsible for what has happened to you...
MICHEL : What madness!

EDMÉE : Yes, yes, you said it in a tone I know all too well... You weren't serious? Tell me you weren't serious! It's as though you had injected me with poison... it's appalling... But to begin with, if you had truly cared for me, you wouldn't have made that offer only once, in a moment of exaltation... you would have spoken of it again.
MICHEL, looking at her fixedly : Are you sure it wasn't because you knew I would speak of it again, and because you were afraid...
EDMÉE : Well?
MICHEL : That you told him everything. It was as if you were hurrying to erect a wall between us.
EDMÉE : I don't understand.
MICHEL : His forbearance, his generosity, which you banked on...
EDMÉE : How could I have banked on them?

MICHEL : ... which you banked on, made your departure impossible. You spoke of risk: but the only true risk, you were far too cowardly to take. You took the easiest way, that of confession. You don't even protest. Because it's blindingly obvious. Oh, I repeat, I hold nothing against you anymore. It has been far too long since... Ah, anyway, love... (He makes a gesture of disgust.) Before I leave, I would need something less worn, less squandered. (He looks toward the side where Osmonde exited; Edmée watches him with anxiety.) And besides...
EDMÉE : You didn't answer my question earlier... When I find myself alone with that thought, it will be dreadful.
MICHEL : What thought?
EDMÉE, burying her head in her hands : The thought that it's partly my fault.

MICHEL : I see, you would very much like me to hand you a clean certificate. Well, I am very sorry, but I cannot... First of all, you lacked imagination far too much. You had no suspicion that I loved you. Oh, you must hear that word without trembling; first because it's terribly long ago, all that, isn't it? And then because it looks a bit too much like a foul disease. But still, if you had had a little more grit and a little less virtue, well! Together the two of us might perhaps have had a life, whereas, well! After your confession... you, I suppose you went to sleep... and I went downhill. One need only look at me. Those are things one doesn't talk about. (He has stood up.) Now listen, I saw just now that you caught my drift. You must let me see that girl from time to time. Oh! Do me the honour of not attributing some sort of sentimentality to me. No, but she intrigues me, it's an idea that distracts me, that's all. And it's hard, at the point I've reached, to find ideas that keep the mind occupied a bit, ideas that aren't...
EDMÉE : You know very well that's impossible. Under what pretext? How could it be explained to her?

MICHEL : Oh, you will tell her anything; do you want me to give her piano lessons? In short, you will look, and you will find something. Goodbye. It is this way, and to the left, isn't it? (He exits; Edmée does not see him out.)
[SCENE V]
EDMÉE, then OSMONDE : (Edmée is prey to great inner turmoil; she sits down, picks up a book, sets it down on the table, stands up, and goes to the upstage door which she holds ajar.)
EDMÉE, to Osmonde : I thought you were in bed. To whom are you writing? Come in for a moment, please. (Osmonde enters, wearing a dressing gown.)
OSMONDE : It seems pointless to start an argument.
EDMÉE : That is not my intention either. Did you go upstairs again just now without our knowledge?
OSMONDE : I made no secret of it. Who is that gentleman leaving just now? Why have you never spoken of him to me?
EDMÉE : He is someone we had completely lost sight of.
OSMONDE : But what an idea, to call on people at such an hour!
EDMÉE : It is to be presumed that this was the only time he could manage...
OSMONDE : Most extraordinary. Papa was quite pale.
EDMÉE : He is feeling a little unwell this evening.
OSMONDE : Then why did you let him go out?
EDMÉE : You know full well your father always does as he pleases. But that is not the issue. I wish to settle the Mégal question once and for all.
OSMONDE : There is no Mégal question.
EDMÉE : Oh! Let us not split hairs, shall we? I have no objection to those girls coming here from time to time, but I forbid you to go upstairs.
OSMONDE : In short, you distrust me. You don't understand that if such a danger existed, your suspicions would only make it worse.
EDMÉE : Who is speaking of danger? Your attitude is improper, that is all.
OSMONDE : And papa, what does he think of it?
EDMÉE : Your father doesn't realize...
OSMONDE : In other words, he doesn't share your prejudice.
EDMÉE : What prejudice, if you please?
OSMONDE : That of belittling me, hurting me, of... Even just now in front of that gentleman, you made me look ridiculous.
EDMÉE : When one is so self-absorbed, one sees only slights and ill treatment everywhere, that is certain. If you devoted to others a tenth of the attention you bestow upon your precious self...
OSMONDE : Mother, I am not selfish.
EDMÉE : That is news to me.

OSMONDE : I am less so than you. You put your heart into nothing you do. And that is all that counts. Attending committees, running a workroom, or knitting socks doesn't prove that one is good. You are not good, you are no better than I am. One has only to look at you when you speak to an invalid; you never smile. All the trouble you take is... is...
EDMÉE : Go on, keep talking.
[SCENE VI]
THE SAME, CLAUDE
CLAUDE, to Osmonde : Still here? Listen, darling, would you be so kind as to make me a cup of tea? I am chilled to the bone... We were freezing at Forstmeyer's...
EDMÉE : And I suppose you achieved nothing.
CLAUDE : We talked.
EDMÉE : Just as I thought... (To Osmonde.) Take the spirit lamp, will you? (Osmonde exits.)
CLAUDE, to Edmée : Did he stay long after I left?
EDMÉE : A few minutes. (A silence.)
CLAUDE : And was Osmonde there the whole time?
EDMÉE : No.
CLAUDE : I think if I had foreseen what it would be like...
EDMÉE : You see, I was right.
CLAUDE : No, that would have been cowardly. But when he spoke of Saint-Loup... and then, I don't know, that cynical air, disgusted with everything...
EDMÉE : He is very ill.
CLAUDE : Yes, I had to keep repeating to myself that he is an unfortunate man.
EDMÉE : Really?
CLAUDE : Otherwise I think I would have told him to leave. The way he looked at the child... you noticed... that above all was what I could not bear.
EDMÉE : Ah, indeed. I see.
CLAUDE : When he came in and took your hand, at first I had the impression of a ghost.
EDMÉE : Yes.
CLAUDE : But afterwards, when he looked at the child, his face came alive... that was worse.
EDMÉE, going to the door : Well, Osmonde!
OSMONDE, offstage : The water isn't boiling yet.
EDMÉE, to Claude : Perhaps we could put a drop of spirits into your tea, no?
CLAUDE : It's not necessary.
EDMÉE, with irony : And I forgot that you signed the famous pledge.
CLAUDE : Couldn't you tell me a little of what he said to you? That is, if it isn't painful for you, of course.
EDMÉE, with sudden feeling : Be demanding, then, be suspicious, be petty; I ask for nothing better.
CLAUDE : What do you mean? (Osmonde enters with a cup of tea which she places on the desk.)
OSMONDE : I put in a lump of sugar. Now I am going to bed. Goodnight, papa, I hope you get warm.
CLAUDE : Goodnight, my darling.
EDMÉE : Goodnight. (Osmonde exits. A silence. Claude drinks his tea.)
EDMÉE : Does that do you good?
CLAUDE : Well?

EDMÉE : Well! Something happened... Claude, I need you. You must help me. You must be able to help me. A dreadful thought is taking root in me. Drive it away... We spoke of what happened long ago; we must not be blamed for it. It was so strange. As though it were yesterday... as though those twenty years had not counted. And yet, he is dying, and I... And so, I discovered that he had been far more unhappy than I believed. Not merely unhappy. In despair. And it was because of that, so it seems, that he led the existence that is now killing him. At least, he believes so. Naturally he may be mistaken. Perhaps in any case... If only I could tell myself that I did the right thing when I confessed everything to you... But he claims... Oh, that cannot be true, it would be too...
CLAUDE : What cannot be true?
EDMÉE : He says I was afraid of him, that I wasn't brave enough to accept life with him, and that it was to chain myself, to bar my own way, that I told you everything.
CLAUDE : I don't understand.

EDMÉE : But yes, because once you knew everything, once you had forgiven me, there could no longer be any question of leaving you. Don't you see? He says I had nothing to fear from you; that I was playing it safe. And it's true, I wasn't afraid of you. That is what is horrible. (With growing bitterness.) Deep down, that evening, I did not speak to you as to my husband.
CLAUDE : Edmée!
EDMÉE : That is the cause of everything. If you had been my husband, if you had loved me as a man loves his wife, with the best and the worst of himself...
CLAUDE : The worst of himself?
EDMÉE : You know full well I would not have betrayed you.
CLAUDE : You are not in your right mind...
EDMÉE : Your voice suddenly rings false.
CLAUDE : The trust you showed in me...
EDMÉE : Trust! The more one loves, the more one mistrusts...
CLAUDE : For hearts such as ours...
EDMÉE : In the first place, that forgiveness which cost you nothing—you had no right to overwhelm me with it.
CLAUDE : Did I not have the right to protect you against yourself?
EDMÉE : Words, mere words. You were judge and party: oh, I don't mean that you loved me. Don't protest... let us say you loved me in God... No, but first of all, there was more than just me.
CLAUDE : Nothing else mattered.
EDMÉE : Your influence over souls? Come, you are not doing yourself justice right now. The scandal of a separation between us...
CLAUDE : Would have fallen upon you alone.
EDMÉE : You don't believe that seriously... And then above all... above all... such a marvellous opportunity to display your evangelical gifts...
CLAUDE, he has risen, ghastly pale : Be quiet.
EDMÉE : Ah! Now you see clearly.
CLAUDE : Be quiet: you are destroying me. (Blank page 110 — End of Act II)
